Q092.L1t: Propositional logic symbolizes whole English sentences as formulas built from sentence letters and connectives such as negation, conjunction and disjunction.
Q092.L2t: In a symbolization, a single sentence letter can stand for a whole claim like "Everybody loves Raymond," and the phrase "or not" can be read as adding the negation of that claim.
Q092.L3t: The sentence offers the claim and its own negation as alternatives, so the right formula joins the letter and its negation with the connective that means "at least one of these holds."
Q092.L4t: The sentence is best symbolized as the letter disjoined with its negation, which is a tautology.
Q092.L2f: Sentence letters in propositional logic can only stand for single names such as Raymond, never for whole claims, and "or not" is always read as a conditional.
Q092.L3f: The phrase "or not" is just a tag that leaves the main claim unchanged, so the sentence asserts only that everybody loves Raymond and needs no connective at all.
Q092.L4f: The best symbolization is just the bare sentence letter L, asserting that everybody loves Raymond.

Q093.L1t: Conditional propositions in logic have two parts, an antecedent and a consequent, and English expresses them with many different connecting phrases.
Q093.L2t: The phrase "only if" is a standard English way of expressing a conditional, and it works differently from the word "if" alone.
Q093.L3t: In an "only if" sentence, the clause that comes before "only if" is the one that implies the clause after it, so the clause after it states a necessary condition and is the consequent.
Q093.L4t: The antecedent is the claim that the university raises tuition.
Q093.L2f: The phrase "only if" is a biconditional that makes the two clauses equivalent, so a conditional with "only if" has no separate antecedent.
Q093.L3f: In an "only if" sentence, the clause that follows the phrase is the one that implies the first clause, so the later conditions such as the trustees' recommendation come first in the conditional's order of implication.
Q093.L4f: The antecedent is the claim that the board of trustees recommends the tuition raise.

Q094.L1t: Predicate logic uses quantifiers, predicate letters and connectives to symbolize English statements about all or some members of a group.
Q094.L2t: Universal statements of the form "All A are B" are normally symbolized with a universal quantifier governing a single conditional, not a conjunction.
Q094.L3t: For "All A are B," the universal quantifier takes a conditional whose antecedent is the predicate of the subject class and whose consequent is the predicate attributed to it, so first-year students must go in the antecedent and the swim test taking in the consequent.
Q094.L4t: The best translation is the universal conditional whose antecedent says x is a first-year student and whose consequent says x takes a swim test.
Q094.L2f: Universal statements of the form "All A are B" are normally symbolized with a universal quantifier governing a disjunction of the two predicates.
Q094.L3f: A universal claim says that each thing has at least one of the two properties named, so "All A are B" is properly symbolized by joining the two predicates with inclusive disjunction.
Q094.L4f: The best translation is the universal quantification of a disjunction saying that everything is either a first-year student or takes a swim test.
